title: Baseball Rugs: What Size to Buy, and Where to Put It
meta_description: Baseball rugs in four sizes, 24"x36" to 60"x96", from $31.90. How to measure a bedroom, playroom or doorway and pick the size that fits.
body_html:
Buy a 36"x60" or 48"x72" baseball rug for beside a bed, a 24"x36" for a doorway or desk, and a 60"x96" to cover a play area. The right one depends on the open floor you measure.

Chillgen's baseball rugs come in those four sizes, from $31.90 for the smallest to $136.90 for the largest. Both designs can be personalized. The sections below help you choose a size with a tape measure instead of guessing. Once you know which size you need, you can compare both designs in all four sizes.

What size baseball rugs are there, and which should I buy?

There are four sizes. The price goes up with the size, so pick the size before you pick the design.

Size (inches)Size (feet)Price fromWho it suits
24" x 36"2' x 3'$31.90A small accent inside a bedroom door, in front of a desk, or beside a toddler bed. Also the cheapest way to try the look.
36" x 60"3' x 5'$66.90A rug along one side of a twin or full bed, so your feet land on it when you get up.
48" x 72"4' x 6'$101.90A bedroom with a wider strip of open floor, or a small reading or play corner.
60" x 96"5' x 8'$136.90A rug that anchors the whole room: under the lower part of a bed, or across the middle of a playroom or den.

The feet column is the inch size divided by 12. Prices are the lowest listed for each size.

All four sizes are rectangles. If you were looking for a round baseball rug, there isn't one in these sizes.

How to apply it: Before you order, mark the rug's outline on the floor with painter's tape and leave it there for a day. Walk around it, open the door over it and pull out the desk chair. A rug that looks right on a product page can still cover a heating vent or catch under a door. The tape shows you that for free.

What to check before deciding

  • The open floor where the rug will go, measured in inches, not estimated.
  • Whether the door swings over that spot.
  • Whether furniture will sit half on and half off the rug, which makes it rock.
  • Which of the four sizes leaves some bare floor around it.

How do I measure for a baseball rug in a bedroom?

A baseball rug in a bedroom usually goes in one of three places, and each one needs a different measurement.

Beside the bed. Measure the gap from the side of the bed to the nearest furniture or wall. The rug's short side has to fit in that gap, so a 36"x60" needs at least 36 inches of open floor and a 48"x72" needs at least 48. The long side then runs along the bed, and you step out of bed onto the rug, not onto bare floor.

Under the lower part of the bed. This is where the 60"x96" earns its price. Lay it across the bed, not along it, so it shows on both sides. To see how much will show, take the bed's width away from 96 inches and halve what's left. That's the strip of rug on each side. If it's narrower than your foot is long, the rug will look like it's hiding under the bed. In that case, a rug beside the bed works better.

At the foot of the bed. Measure from the foot of the bed to the opposite wall or dresser. A 24"x36" or 36"x60" laid across the foot works if the bed frame doesn't overhang where the rug sits.

Wherever it goes, the bed legs should sit fully on the rug or fully off it. Legs on the edge make a rug curl and slide out of place.

What to check before deciding

  • The bed's width and length, measured from the frame, not the mattress.
  • The gap between the bed and the next piece of furniture.
  • Where the bed legs will land compared with the rug's edge.
  • The path from the door to the bed, so the rug doesn't sit where people trip over its corner.

Where else does a baseball area rug or baseball carpet work?

First, the difference people often ask about. A "baseball carpet" in most searches means one of these: a loose area rug with a baseball design. Fitted wall-to-wall carpet is something else. A loose rug can be lifted, moved to another room later, or taken with you when you move.

Outside the bedroom, the size follows the job the rug has to do.

Inside a door or at an entry. The 24"x36" (from $31.90) is the smallest of the four, so it's the easiest to fit inside a doorway. Measure the clearance under the door when it's closed and open. If the door scrapes the rug, move the rug back or choose a spot past the swing.

Under a desk chair. The rug needs to be big enough that the chair stays on it when someone pushes back. Measure the desk's width, then how far the chair rolls back in normal use. A 36"x60" laid lengthwise along the desk covers more than a 24"x36" turned the same way, but your measurements settle it.

Playroom, den or basement. This is where the 60"x96" makes sense. Leave a strip of floor showing on every side, and keep it clear of anything that has to open, such as cupboards or a toy chest lid.

Both product pages describe a "non-slip backing to prevent dangerous movements and slips." Neither the backing's floor types nor the care method appear in what we've published here. Read the product page for both before you order, especially if the rug is going on carpet or somewhere that gets messy.

What to check before deciding

  • Door clearance at the spot you have in mind, with the door closed and open.
  • How far the chair rolls back, if the rug goes under a desk.
  • Your floor type, checked against the backing details on the product page.
  • What has to open or move near the rug.

Vintage or Space: which design, and what should you personalize?

There are two designs. Both start at $31.90, and both product pages say each one "supports custom options for a personalized home touch."

The Personalized Vintage Baseball Rug uses a vintage baseball pattern. The Personalized Space Baseball Rug puts the baseball theme in a space setting. The product photos are the best guide to their colors, so open both side by side before you decide.

To choose between them, put the product photo next to a photo of the room: the bedding, the wall color and whatever is already on the floor. A rug that picks up one color already in the room usually looks planned. One that brings in a new color has to carry the room on its own.

For personalization, settle the wording before you open the product page. [NEED: which fields can be customized, e.g. name, number or text line, and any character limits] Check the spelling with whoever the rug is for. Then decide where the text should be read from: the bed, the door, or standing over it.

What to check before deciding

  • The size, chosen first, since it moves the price more than the design does.
  • The exact spelling of any name or text.
  • Which way the text should face once the rug is down.
  • Whether the design's colors work with the bedding and walls.

Worked example: one rug for a small bedroom

This is a made-up room, used to show the decision. It isn't a customer's room.

The room: a twin bed against one wall and a desk against the opposite wall. Measured across the floor from the bed frame to the front of the desk, the gap is wider than 36 inches but narrower than 48.

Step 1: compare the gap with each rug's short side. The rug lies beside the bed, so its short side has to fit across the gap.

Step 2: rule sizes out.

  • 60"x96": its 60-inch short side is wider than the gap. It could only go under the bed, and in a room this tight it would run under the desk too.
  • 48"x72": its 48-inch short side is also wider than the gap, so the desk would sit on the rug's edge and the chair would rock.
  • 24"x36": it fits easily, but its 36-inch length covers only a small patch beside the bed.

Step 3: choose. The 36"x60" is the one size left. Its short side fits the gap with bare floor to spare before the desk, and its 60-inch length runs along the bed where feet land. It starts at $66.90.

Step 4: test it. Tape a 36-by-60-inch rectangle beside the bed. Open the bedroom door, pull the desk chair out and walk from the door to the bed. If nothing catches, that's the size to order.
